title: Opus 5 High as default is probably overkill
author: Moist_Signal_5080
selftext:
Maybe I’m late to realize this but I found “high” setting was overkill. I switched to low or medium and got done in 2 days (using 22% of my weekly), what would typically max out my weekly usage.

As a person who never made a game or did any sort of coding, I didn’t know what was necessary. I just kinda figured coding is probably hard, might as well use High effort just in case.

After a little research that’s how it works. If you have your your next feature planned out, leaving nothing open ended or up for interpretation, low setting is perfectly fine. My incorrect assumption was “coding is probably difficult so I’ll use high, must be the default for a reason”.

Maybe I’m wrong, but it’s working much better for me this way.

comments.author: broker415
comments.body: Yeah I scope and plan in a strong model on high and then depending if I’m in Claude or cursor I’ll use a much more “daily driver” class model for the actual building especially if it’s a simple change in a project that already has well engineered context

comments.author: Time_Cat_5212
comments.body:
Opus 5 is spray and pray, and on high or extra it's just going to create a ton of unnecessary work

replies.author: Moist_Signal_5080
replies.body: Opus 5 high was getting the job done, but it took way longer and burnt through my usage like crazy.

comments.author: ishmaellius
comments.body:
Opus 5 on high likes building lots of verification code.  If you aren't watching it closely it spins up 2-3 different testing harnesses for every little thing you have it implement.  

Sometimes this is useful in the context of careful surgical edits, but when you're building largely greenfield or experimenting with something you're not sure you'll keep, it absolutely slows down development. 

I've started scanning specs for this and telling it which pieces are actually worth developing these tests for vs what is experimental and acceptance is literally me running and seeing something to say if it passes or not.

This has helped quite a bit for me.

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body: This has absolutely nothing to do with the reasoning level you set it to.

replies.author: ishmaellius
replies.body: Your mileage may vary, I find medium opus 5 doesn't test every little thing

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body: Even if true, how is that a good thing?

replies.author: ishmaellius
replies.body:
You must not do a whole lot of practical development.

Here I'll spell it out for you - tokens spent making and running test suites on things you're not even sure you'll keep is wasted time and tokens.

I don't need a test verifying a tree prop is visible if I don't even know if I want a tree there. 

AI can't often tell what's more important or more experimental for you, and if you let it just go off and do whatever, it'll waste a lot of time and tokens.

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
That example is not a question of IF you should have tests, but WHAT tests,  and how you make sure you get the right kind of tests. You can control that to some extent, and you should spend time thinking about that, rather than just letting the AI write "trust me bro" tests to fulfill a coverage quota, or make the AI stupid so it can't write tests (but also fails at other things).

* Have rules for what tests to write and not to write
* Have a workflow that includes test sanity and coverage in code review. Not the shitty lines of code counting coverage of yore, but AI reasoning about what actually needs to be covered and how.
* Have a good testing toolchain
* Keep tests well-maintained at all times, so a crappy test regime doesn't become the repo pattern that agents keep following.
* Make test design part of the planning and design process fir every festure or increment.

comments.body: Sonnet for code then opus for QC?

comments.author: RipstarGaming
comments.body: It depends on the complexity of the task. Some tasks can only be correctly handled with Fable 5 Ultracode, while others Opus is plenty

comments.author: vurt72
comments.body:
Yeah, you can use the higher settings for planning, then let a more simple model to the work.  
Use Token savers. e.g RTK and TOKF.  
Understand how the cache works or you will also lose a lot of tokens. 

I code from morning to late at night with Claude, i can do that for many, many days. It's wild to see some people saying they use up all tokens in like 30 mins etc. It's impossible unless you are absolutely clueless.
